snippet.title: Navigating the Great AI Transition
snippet.description:
Katie Couric sits down with futurist Amy Webb — founder and CEO of the Future Today Strategy Group and professor at NYU Stern — to unpack what she calls a technological "supercycle." AI, robotics and biotech are converging in a way that's never happened before, and for the first time in history, economies can grow without leaning on large pools of human labor. So what happens to work, stability and our sense of human value when the old rules stop applying?
Webb pushes back on the idea that we're stuck choosing between AI utopia and AI doom. Instead, she and Katie dig into the real question: how do we actually help people and institutions adapt as this shift accelerates?
This conversation was recorded live at the Aspen Ideas Festival, the Aspen Institute's signature summer gathering of business and civic leaders, innovators, scholars and changemakers exploring this year's theme, "Declarations of Independence."

snippet.title: The Most Extreme Economic Experiment in History
snippet.description:
This video tells the tragic story of the most extreme communist system that ever existed. 

This is the dark story of the Cambodian Holocaust. And it didn't even happen very long ago. 

Following the turbulence of the Vietnam War, in which Cambodia was unwillingly dragged in, a military insurgency group called the Khmer Rouge took power in Cambodia. They were led by a cruel and mysterious figure named Pol Pot. They were Communists - and they were the most extreme form of Communists that have ever existed. 

The Khmer Rouge took the capital Phnom Penh, and began enacted a series of heinous and cruel "reforms". They had a utopian notion they could bring Cambodia back to an idyllic farming society. What happened was the opposite of a utopia. 

The Khmer Rouge genocide acts as a warning as to the dangers of Communism, and the dangers of tyrannical governments and revolutions.

snippet.title: YC Spring 26 Batch Breakdown & Takeaways
snippet.description:
A few observations and takeaways from this Y Combinator Spring 2026 batch

🤖 Every company is an AI company now (173 of 196 lead with AI or agents, and only 23 don’t mention it at all)
🏢 It’s overwhelmingly B2B - about 61% sell to businesses vs. just 6% consumer
👷 It’s an engineer’s batch: 70% of founders are technical, ~half the companies are all-technical teams, and only 3% are dropouts.
🏭 Hardware is back. Industrials (defense, robotics, energy) jumped from ~2% of YC three years ago to 13%, with 11 in defense alone.
📞 ~11% build for a customer that isn’t human, building infrastructure for agents
💼 At least 17 companies are AI-native services, going after consulting and back-office budgets.

snippet.title: Gold VS Bitcoin
snippet.description:
While Bitcoin gets a lot of attention, it hasn’t played the safe-haven role many expected. In my view, there are a few reasons why.

First, Bitcoin lacks privacy. Transactions can be monitored and potentially controlled, which is why central banks aren’t looking to hold it.

Second, it also has a high correlation with tech stocks. When investors get squeezed in other areas of their portfolio, they sell their Bitcoin to cover it.

Third, it’s a relatively small and controllable market, whereas gold stands alone. There is only one gold.

Ultimately, gold is more widely held, deeply established, and still plays a central role in the global system.

snippet.title: Why a Record Stock Market Only Makes (Some) People Rich
snippet.description:
Owning stocks and getting rich from stocks are two completely different things.

Millions of Americans technically own stocks today. But the size of your portfolio determines whether a record market feels like a life-changing payday or just enough to cover a few bills.

It sounds obvious, but that's the part almost every headline leaves out.

The same market can hand one household enough for a weekend getaway, while handing another enough for a down payment on a house. 

That's why record highs don't feel the same to everyone.

snippet.title: Gold Is A Very Selective Diversifier
snippet.description:
Gold is the world’s oldest money and remains the second-largest reserve asset held by central banks.

Its true value lies in what it isn’t: it is not a fiat currency. Because of this, it serves as a powerful diversifier when conditions are bad for ordinary financial assets.

Most investors make the mistake of trying to "time" the market—jumping between stocks, bonds, and gold. Even for professionals, that is a losing game. The better approach? Build a balanced, highly diversified strategic asset allocation that can weather any environment.

snippet.title: Principles Behind 250 Years Of American Success
snippet.description:
When you look back over the last 250 years, the United States has been an amazing place that has given people equal opportunity. People came from all over to work and live well together, becoming prosperous because you could have a good balance of freedom, rule of law, and civility. People were willing to compromise and work together because they recognized that, while imperfect, the greater system was ultimately fair.

Our founding fathers had an aspirational dream of what could be possible, and that dream became a reality. It is one hell of an accomplishment, and we must not lose sight of the principles behind that success.

Which principles do you think have contributed most to America’s success?
